background.definition: Laryngeal cancer is a malignancy of the larynx. Most laryngeal malignancies are squamous cell carcinomas.

list.listitem: In 2023, 12,380 new cases of laryngeal cancer and 3820 deaths from laryngeal cancer occurred in the United States.
Laryngeal carcinoma is the 11th most common form of cancer among males, worldwide.
Surgery to treat late-stage disease may require a traumatic partial or total laryngectomy, with a wide-ranging impact on patients and families.
Smoking
Heavy alcohol consumption (distilled spirits)
Link to human papillomavirus (HPV) infections, synergistic with tobacco use
Squamous cell carcinoma of the larynx is most common in males older than 55 years with a history of smoking and heavy alcohol consumption.
Causally related to human papillomavirus (HPV) infection.
The disease is divided into four major stages (I-IV). Each of these is divided by location: supraglottic, glottic, or subglottic.
Prognosis is better for stages I and II and for supraglottic cancers.
Smoking cessation and decreasing alcohol consumption to moderate levels are recommended to prevent laryngeal cancer. C
Routine population screening or screening of asymptomatic individuals in high-risk groups is not addressed by the United States Preventive Services Task Force. C

The preferred initial diagnostic study is direct laryngoscopy with biopsy. C

list.listitem: Common symptoms in patients with laryngeal cancer include blood in sputum, vocal changes, swallowing problems, and halitosis. Patients may also complain about ear pain, fatigue, or expectoration of tissue.
On physical examination, note vocal changes, hoarseness, or new breath odors.
Evaluate the patient for weight loss and fatigue.
Evaluate neck mobility and examine for neck masses; also examine the oral pharynx and epiglottic tip.
The recommended initial study if laryngeal cancer is suspected is laryngoscopy with biopsy.

All patients with biopsy-confirmed glottic or supraglottic laryngeal cancer should have a CXR or chest CT (the latter if at high risk for thoracic metastases) and CT with contrast and thin cuts or MRI of primary tumor and neck. Also consider dental and speech/swallowing evaluations.
There is increasing evidence for use of PET-CT in staging and in post treatment evaluation of response.
Suspect laryngeal cancer in patients with hoarseness, vocal changes, weight loss, or difficulty in swallowing for at least 2 weeks.
The initial diagnostic study is laryngoscopy.
Treatment requires multidisciplinary planning, often with more than one modality of therapy (surgery, radiation and chemotherapy).
Surgery and radiation therapy remain the first choice in treatment of laryngeal carcinoma. A
For locally advanced disease in fit patients, concurrent chemoradiation achieves improved outcomes.
Choice of total versus partial laryngectomy, use of radiation as definitive treatment, and degree of neck dissection depend on tumor stage, extent of spread, and patient factors.

Treatment generally involves surgery and radiation therapy. Laryngeal function preservation is of prime importance, and several function-preserving surgical techniques are now available. A systematic review found 17 retrospective studies, and concluded that there was no survival benefit to total laryngectomy over nonsurgical modalities. However, the ability to draw conclusions is limited by the non-randomized, retrospective nature of the included studies.

A systematic review of 42 trials assessing functional outcome with early stage laryngeal cancer (T1 and T2 tumours) found no clear benefits for either endoscopic laser surgery or external beam radiation as primary treatment.

A Cochrane review found only a single randomized trial that compared surgery with radiotherapy in patients with early-stage laryngeal cancer. Additional studies are underway. The recommendations given below are drawn from National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines.

Severe dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, or T1/T2 disease: these can usually be managed with radiation therapy or partial laryngectomy. Neck dissection and/or radiation therapy is recommended if there is nodal involvement.

T3 disease: most patients require total laryngectomy. Those with nodal involvement require a greater degree of neck dissection. The alternative is radiation therapy + cisplatin, followed by either observation if response is complete, salvage surgery if residual primary tumor exists, or neck dissection for complete response at primary site but residual tumor elsewhere.

T4 disease: if resectable, total laryngectomy with degree of dissection and resection of the thyroid is determined by the degree of nodal involvement. A meta-analysis of 15 studies with a total of 6288 patients compared laryngectomy with organ preservation therapy; the results suggest that survival may be improved with surgery but only in patients with T4 disease. Selected patients may consider chemoradiation followed by observation, neck dissection, or salvage surgery depending on response.

T1 and T2 disease: primary therapy is endoscopic resection ± selective neck dissection, open partial supraglottic laryngectomy ± selective neck dissection, or definitive radiation therapy. Consider chemoradiation or radiation as adjuvant therapy.

T3 and T4a without cartilage destruction and with low volume base of tongue involvement: (1) laryngectomy, ipsilateral thyroidectomy, and selective neck dissection followed by adjuvant radiation or chemoradiation; or (2) concurrent chemoradiation followed by salvage surgery if needed.
T4a with cartilage destruction or high volume base of tongue involvement: laryngectomy, ipsilateral thyroidectomy, and selective neck dissection followed by adjuvant radiation or chemoradiation.
See NCCN guidelines for management of unresectable and node-positive supraglottic disease.
Experimental use of gene therapy has been reported.

A systematic review of 21 trials and 5630 patients investigated the risk of occult metastases in squamous laryngeal cancer and concluded that those patients with clinically node negative disease but T3/4 tumours should receive elective neck treatment because of high risk of occult nodal involvement.
The normal complications and consequences of surgery and radiation therapy are seen.

Complications specific to treatment of laryngeal cancer include loss of upper body strength, psychosocial trauma, limited mobility of the neck, voice loss in some procedures, radiation-induced neoplasms of the neck, chronic pain, breathing difficulties, and stomal infections or malignancies.
Prognosis is better for stages I and II and for supraglottic cancers. B
Regular follow-up and monitoring are recommended to monitor for recurrence. B
Prognosis is better for stages I and II and for supraglottic cancers. B
Early-stage diseases (T1 and T2) have an 80% to 90% probability of cure; for more advanced disease, cure rates are 60% or less. B
For supraglottic cancer, the 5-year survival is 30% to 95%, depending on stage; for glottic cancer, it is 40% to 97%. B
Recommendations for follow-up and monitoring are from the NCCN guidelines.
Physical examination every 1 to 3 months during year 1, every 2 to 4 months during year 2, every 4 to 6 months during years 3 to 5, and every 6 to 12 months beyond that.
Chest imaging is indicated based on symptoms.
Determine thyroid-stimulating hormone level every 6 to 12 months if the neck was irradiated.
Speech and swallowing evaluation and rehabilitation are given as needed.
